lines.speaker: reader
lines.text: Someone's staring at you. Hard. Waiting for you to look away.

lines.speaker: reader
lines.text: Most people do one of two things. Stare back. Or stare at the floor.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: In 1972, researchers stood at intersections and stared at drivers waiting at red lights.
lines.say: In nineteen seventy-two, researchers stood at intersections and stared at drivers waiting at red lights.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: When the light turned green, the drivers who were stared at sped away faster.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Your brain reads a long stare as a challenge, or a threat. It wants you to move.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A stare puts your body on alert. That's the whole trick.

lines.speaker: reader
lines.text: So don't play his game. Here's what I do.

lines.speaker: reader
lines.text: One. Breathe out slowly and relax your face. Calm reads as confident.

lines.speaker: reader
lines.text: Two. Meet his eyes for one second, with a small nod. Like you just noticed him.

lines.speaker: reader
lines.text: Three. Look away slowly. Not down. To the side, like he's not that interesting.

lines.speaker: reader
lines.text: Still staring? Ask him, friendly and out loud: can I help you?

lines.speaker: reader
lines.text: Stares only work in silence. And if it ever feels dangerous, skip all of this and leave.

lines.speaker: reader
lines.text: Comment the weirdest stare you've ever gotten. I'll read them.

lines.speaker: reader
lines.text: Tomorrow: what to do when someone stands too close.
